messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Robert's Accident

Robert Castellano was fifty-four when a delivery truck ran a red light at the intersection of Fifth and Morrison, T-boning his sedan on the driver's side. He remembered the sound first—a compressed metal scream, the window exploding inward, his own voice somewhere distant and strange. The truck's bumper crushed the door frame; his left shoulder dislocated on impact, his ribs cracked, and for three seconds that felt like hours, he couldn't draw breath. When the paramedics extracted him, his hands were shaking so violently they had to strap him to the gurney. The hospital stay lasted nine days. The physical recovery took months of physical therapy, but the accident itself—the moment of absolute helplessness, the knowledge that his body had betrayed him utterly, that he had nearly died in broad daylight—that never left.

In the first weeks after discharge, Robert tried to return to his life as an interior designer. His firm, which he'd built over thirty years, had clients waiting. He could work from home, make site visits, oversee installations. But something had shifted. When he sat at his desk to review fabric swatches and floor plans, his mind would catch on small sounds—a car horn from the street below, the rumble of a delivery vehicle—and his body would flood with adrenaline. His heart would hammer. His breathing would shallow. He had come to believe that his body could no longer be trusted to keep him safe, that it might fail him again without warning, and this terror lived beneath every waking moment.

The triggers multiplied. Three weeks after coming home, a client wanted to reschedule a consultation because she'd been in a fender-bender. Robert listened to her describe the impact, the moment of fear, and felt his stomach drop. He made an excuse—a migraine, a scheduling conflict—and cancelled. Within a month, he'd stopped accepting new projects that required site visits. When colleagues or friends mentioned accidents, even casually, his chest would tighten. He'd excuse himself, citing fatigue or work pressure. By autumn, he'd noticed that even photographs in design magazines—a sleek car, a street scene—could trigger a wave of panic that left him shaky and withdrawn.

By the following winter, Robert's world had contracted significantly. He stopped driving altogether, relying on Uber, though the experience of sitting in a stranger's car, unable to control the vehicle or predict what might happen, filled him with dread. He began turning down projects that required leaving his apartment. His firm, sensing his withdrawal, had offered him a transition to a consulting role, but Robert knew the real problem wasn't his work capacity—it was that he no longer recognized himself. The man who had once thrived on site visits, on the energy of construction sites and client meetings, had become someone who flinched at traffic sounds and avoided the street. What frightened him most was the permanence of it. He was certain he had changed for the worse, that this version of himself—anxious, limited, trapped—was who he would be forever. His ex-wife, with whom he'd remained cordial, commented after a video call that he seemed "diminished somehow." He didn't argue.

Now, at fifty-seven, Robert had spent three years managing his life around the accident. He worked from home exclusively, communicating with clients by email and video. He lived on the third floor of a building with a back entrance, which meant he could avoid the main street when he left. He'd stopped seeing friends who lived across town. The panic attacks had become less frequent—perhaps because he'd eliminated so many situations that triggered them—but they hadn't disappeared. What finally brought him to seek help was a realization that struck him one morning while reviewing a design proposal: he couldn't remember the last time he'd felt capable, the last time he'd trusted his own judgment or his body's ability to move through the world without catastrophe. He was living a life of avoidance, and it was a life he no longer recognized as his own.
